title: Von Neumann Architecture and Memory Hierarchy
content: The Von Neumann architecture is a theoretical computer design published in 1945 where program instructions and data share a common read-write memory storage and bus. Core components include: 1) Central Processing Unit (Arithmetic Logic Unit and Control Unit with Program Counter and Instruction Registers); 2) Main Memory (RAM); 3) Mass external storage; 4) Input/Output mechanisms. Modern CPUs mitigate the 'Von Neumann Bottleneck' (throughput limit between CPU and memory) using multi-level SRAM cache hierarchies (L1, L2, L3 caches), hardware prefetching, out-of-order execution, and branch prediction.

sources.name: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach

title: Virtual Memory, Paging, and the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
content: Virtual memory provides an abstraction of contiguous, uniform address spaces to each process while providing hardware isolation and enabling programs to exceed physical RAM capacity. The operating system and Memory Management Unit (MMU) divide virtual address space into fixed-size chunks called 'pages' (typically 4KB) mapped to physical 'page frames' via hierarchical page tables. The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is an on-chip hardware cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address translations to avoid multi-level memory lookups. A 'page fault' occurs when an accessed virtual page is not resident in physical RAM, triggering an interrupt that loads the page from disk swap.

sources.name: Operating System Concepts

title: OSI 7-Layer Model and TCP/IP Architecture
content: Network communications are conceptualized across standardized layers: The OSI reference model defines 7 layers: 1) Physical (bits, cables, signaling); 2) Data Link (frames, MAC addresses, Ethernet, switches); 3) Network (packets, IP addresses, routers); 4) Transport (segments, TCP reliable byte-stream / UDP datagrams, port numbers); 5) Session; 6) Presentation; 7) Application (HTTP, DNS, SSH). The practical TCP/IP suite consolidates layers 5-7 into the Application layer. TCP ensures reliability through a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), sequence numbers, sliding window flow control, and congestion control algorithms (CUBIC, BBR).

sources.name: Computer Networks: A Systems Approach

title: ACID Properties and Brewer's CAP Theorem
content: In database systems, ACID guarantees transaction reliability: Atomicity (all-or-nothing execution); Consistency (preserves database schema constraints); Isolation (concurrent transactions execute without interference, with serializability being the highest level); Durability (committed transactions survive system crashes). In distributed data systems, Eric Brewer's CAP Theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of three guarantees during a network partition: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write), Availability (every non-failing node returns a response), and Partition Tolerance (system operates despite arbitrary message drops).

sources.name: Designing Data-Intensive Applications

title: TLS 1.3 Protocol and Modern Cryptographic Primitives
content: Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3, RFC 8446) encrypts Internet communications across the Transport layer. Key security innovations include: 1) 1-RTT handshake (and optional 0-RTT resumption); 2) Complete removal of legacy weak ciphers (RC4, 3DES, CBC mode, SHA-1); 3) Mandatory Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDHE) ensuring Forward Secrecy—even if a server's private key is compromised in the future, past session traffic cannot be decrypted; 4) Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 for simultaneous confidentiality and integrity.

sources.name: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

title: Concurrency, Race Conditions, and Coffman's Deadlock Conditions
content: Concurrent programs require synchronization primitives (mutexes, semaphores, atomic operations) to avoid race conditions—where the output is dependent on non-deterministic thread execution timing. A deadlock occurs when a set of concurrent processes are permanently blocked waiting for resources held by one another. Edward G. Coffman Jr. identified the four necessary and sufficient conditions for deadlock: 1) Mutual Exclusion (unshareable resources); 2) Hold and Wait (processes hold resources while requesting others); 3) No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly confiscated); 4) Circular Wait (a closed chain of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next). Deadlock prevention eliminates at least one condition (e.g. strict resource ordering).

sources.name: System Deadlocks

title: Fundamental Algorithms, Big-O Complexity, and Dijkstra's Shortest Path
content: Asymptotic analysis (Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta) quantifies the worst-case, best-case, and average-case scaling of algorithms as input size N grows. Fundamental algorithmic paradigms include: 1) Divide and Conquer: MergeSort and QuickSort achieving O(N log N) optimal comparison sorting; 2) Dynamic Programming: memoization and tabulation breaking overlapping subproblems into polynomial-time solutions (Knapsack, Bellman-Ford); 3) Greedy Algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm finds single-source shortest paths on non-negative weighted graphs in O((V + E) log V) using a priority queue (min-heap); 4) Complexity Classes: P (polynomial-time solvable), NP (polynomial-time verifiable), and NP-Complete problems (Cook-Levin Theorem, 3-SAT) for which no known polynomial algorithm exists.

sources.name: Introduction to Algorithms (CLRS)

title: Fundamental Data Structures: Hash Tables, Balanced Trees, and B-Trees
content: Data structures organize memory for efficient algorithmic access: 1) Hash Tables: provide O(1) expected average lookup, insertion, and deletion by mapping keys to array buckets via hash functions, resolving collisions with chaining or open addressing (Robin Hood, cuckoo hashing); 2) Self-Balancing Binary Search Trees: AVL trees and Red-Black trees maintain O(log N) worst-case balance by applying tree rotations; 3) B-Trees and B+ Trees (Bayer & McCreight, 1970): self-balancing multi-way search trees optimized for disk and block storage (databases and filesystems like InnoDB, Ext4, NTFS) where nodes match disk page sizes to minimize expensive I/O operations.

sources.name: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol 3: Sorting and Searching

title: Compiler Architecture, Abstract Syntax Trees (AST), LLVM, and JIT
content: Compilers translate high-level programming languages into executable machine code through distinct frontend and backend phases: 1) Frontend: Lexical analysis (tokenization) converts character streams into tokens; Syntactic analysis (parsing) verifies grammatical structure and constructs an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST); Semantic analysis enforces type-checking and symbol resolution; 2) Intermediate Representation (IR): Decouples language frontends from hardware backends (pioneered by Chris Lattner's LLVM infrastructure), applying target-independent optimizations (dead code elimination, loop unrolling, SSA form); 3) Backend: Instruction selection, register allocation (graph coloring), and machine code generation; 4) Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilers: Dynamically profile running bytecode (JVM HotSpot, V8) to compile hot execution paths directly into optimized native machine code at runtime.

sources.name: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book)

title: Distributed Consensus: Paxos, Raft, and Byzantine Fault Tolerance
content: Distributed consensus allows a cluster of independent nodes to agree on state transitions despite network delays, packet drops, and node crashes: 1) Paxos (Leslie Lamport, 1998): guarantees safety under asynchronous networks using multi-phase commit (Prepare, Promise, Propose, Accept); 2) Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014): decomposes consensus into understandable, distinct subproblems—Leader Election, Log Replication, and Safety—using randomized election timers and strong leader authority, powering etcd, Consul, and Kubernetes; 3) Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT): tolerates malicious or arbitrary Byzantine failures (up to f < n/3 faulty nodes), standard in cryptographic ledgers and distributed networks.

sources.name: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (USENIX ATC 2014)
sources.publisher: Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, Stanford University

title: Software Engineering Principles: SOLID, Design Patterns, and CI/CD
content: Software engineering governs the reliable design, construction, and maintenance of complex software systems: 1) SOLID Principles (Robert C. Martin): Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion; 2) Design Patterns (Gang of Four): Creational (Singleton, Factory, Builder), Structural (Adapter, Decorator, Facade), and Behavioral (Observer, Strategy, Command); 3) Architectural Paradigms: Monolithic architectures provide operational simplicity and low network latency; Microservices decompose applications into independently deployable services communicating over gRPC or REST, requiring distributed tracing and eventual consistency; 4) Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD): automated pipelines that compile code, execute unit/integration test suites, and enforce static analysis before deploying to production environments.

sources.name: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software

title: Moore's Law, Dennard Scaling, and Modern Semiconductor Physics
content: Moore's Law was an empirical observation made by Gordon Moore in 1965, predicting that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles roughly every two years, accompanied by declining cost per transistor. For decades, Dennard scaling (constant power density as transistors shrank) ensured clock speed increases alongside density gains. However, Dennard scaling ended around 2005 due to leakage currents. Modern consensus on Moore's Law is divided: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared 'Moore's Law is dead' because traditional monolithic 2D transistor scaling has slowed, costs per wafer have soared at 3nm/2nm nodes, and quantum tunneling limits gate thickness. Conversely, Intel and TSMC assert Moore's Law continues through architectural innovations: Gate-All-Around (GAA) nanosheet transistors (RibbonFET), backside power delivery (PowerVia), 3D packaging, and chiplet modularization.

title: Comparison of RAM (Random Access Memory) and ROM (Read-Only Memory)
content: RAM (Random Access Memory) and ROM (Read-Only Memory) are foundational primary memory types with contrasting operational characteristics: 1) Volatility: RAM is volatile memory that requires continuous electrical power to maintain state, losing all stored data when powered down, whereas ROM is non-volatile memory that retains stored instructions and data permanently without electrical power. 2) Read/Write Capabilities: RAM supports high-speed read and write operations by the CPU during active program execution, whereas ROM is read-only during standard operation (or altered only through specialized reprogramming like EEPROM or Flash). 3) Primary Purpose: RAM serves as temporary working memory holding operating system processes, active runtime data structures, and application execution code; ROM stores permanent system firmware, bootstrap code (BIOS/UEFI), and essential microcode required to initialize hardware upon startup.

sources.name: Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface

title: How Android Studio Builds an Android Application (Gradle Build System and APK Pipeline)
content: Android Studio compiles and builds Android applications through a multi-stage deterministic pipeline orchestrated by the Gradle build system and the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP): 1) Resource Compilation: The Android Asset Packaging Tool 2 (AAPT2) parses and compiles XML layouts, drawables, strings, and manifest files into binary format, emitting the R.java class containing integer resource IDs. 2) Source Code Compilation: The Kotlin compiler (kotlinc) and Java compiler (javac) compile source code into standard JVM .class bytecode files. 3) Desugaring and Dexing: The D8 and R8 compiler desugars modern Java 8+ language features and translates .class bytecode into Dalvik Executable (.dex) bytecode designed for the Android Runtime (ART) and Dalvik virtual machine, performing dead-code stripping, tree shaking, and class shrinking. 4) Packaging: The apkbuilder bundles compiled resources (.arsc), DEX files, and native C/C++ shared libraries (.so) into an unsigned Android Package (APK) or Android App Bundle (AAB). 5) Optimization and Signing: The zipalign utility aligns uncompressed data on 4-byte boundaries to reduce memory overhead, and apksigner cryptographically signs the archive with V2, V3, or V4 signature schemes for secure device deployment.

sources.name: Android Developers: Configure Your Build

title: Python Decorators Architecture, Higher-Order Functions, and Closures
content: In Python, a decorator is a design pattern and syntactic feature (denoted by the '@decorator' prefix above a callable definition) that dynamically extends or modifies the behavior of a function, method, or class without altering its source code. Under the hood, decorators are higher-order functions that take a callable as an argument and return a wrapped callable. They rely on Python's first-class functions, lexical scoping, and closures to capture arguments and preserve state. The standard library 'functools.wraps' helper is typically used on the inner wrapper function to preserve original function attributes such as __name__, __doc__, and type annotations. Decorators are widely utilized across Python ecosystems for logging, authentication, caching/memoization (e.g., functools.lru_cache), rate-limiting, timing metrics, and framework routing (e.g., Flask and FastAPI route decorators).

sources.name: Python Language Reference: Compound Statements (Decorators)

title: Unreal Engine Architecture, Systems, and Capabilities
content: Unreal Engine is an advanced real-time 3D creation tool and game engine developed by Epic Games. Built on a high-performance modular C++ codebase, Unreal Engine is structured around several core architectural systems: 1) Gameplay Framework: An object-oriented hierarchy rooted in UObject, with AActor representing world-spawned entities, APawn/ACharacter for controllable agents, and UActorComponent for modular behaviors; 2) Build Automation: The UnrealHeaderTool (UHT) parses UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION reflection macros to generate code for garbage collection, serialization, and network replication, while UnrealBuildTool (UBT) orchestrates native compilation; 3) Visual Scripting (Blueprints): A comprehensive node-based visual programming language compiled into fast virtual machine bytecode or nativized C++; 4) Graphics and Rendering: Nanite virtualized micropolygon geometry allowing film-quality source meshes, Lumen dynamic global illumination and reflections, and Virtual Shadow Maps; 5) Simulation and Audio: Chaos physics simulation, Niagara programmable visual effects, and MetaSounds procedural audio system.

sources.name: Unreal Engine Documentation: Architecture and Core Systems

title: How Unity Works: Game Engine Architecture, Lifecycle, and Runtimes
content: Unity is a cross-platform real-time 3D and 2D development platform developed by Unity Technologies. Unity operates primarily on a Component-Entity architecture where GameObjects act as containers for modular components derived from MonoBehaviour. Key operational systems include: 1) Deterministic Execution Loop: Game logic executes along a strictly ordered lifecycle, advancing through Awake, OnEnable, Start, FixedUpdate (physics tick), Update (frame tick), LateUpdate (camera tracking), and rendering passes. 2) Scripting and Compilation: Developers write C# scripts executed via the Mono runtime in development and ahead-of-time (AOT) compiled into optimized native C++ machine code using the IL2CPP toolchain for target platforms. 3) Rendering Pipelines: Scriptable Render Pipelines (SRP) including Universal Render Pipeline (URP) for performant multi-platform graphics and High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) for photorealistic compute-driven visuals. 4) High-Performance Tech: The Unity C# Job System and Burst Compiler leverage data-oriented technology stack (DOTS) to compile vectorized, multi-threaded native assembly.

sources.name: Unity User Manual: Order of Execution for Event Functions

title: Machine Learning Foundations, Paradigms, and Core Concepts
content: Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of artificial intelligence and computer science focused on building mathematical algorithms and statistical models that learn patterns and rules directly from training data rather than requiring explicit manual programming. Machine learning is organized into three primary paradigms: 1) Supervised Learning: Models (Linear Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Neural Networks) learn a functional mapping from feature inputs to known ground-truth targets for classification or regression; 2) Unsupervised Learning: Discovering inherent latent patterns, clusters, or probability distributions in unlabeled data via techniques like K-Means clustering, Gaussian Mixture Models, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA); 3) Reinforcement Learning: Autonomous agents learning optimal behavioral policies by taking actions in an environment to maximize cumulative reward signals through Markov Decision Processes. Modern deep learning extends these principles through multi-layer artificial neural networks and Transformer architectures trained via backpropagation and gradient descent optimization.

sources.name: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

title: Quantum Computing Principles, Superposition, Entanglement, and Qubits
content: Quantum computing is a revolutionary computing paradigm that harnesses the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics to process information exponentially faster than classical computers for specific computational problem classes. Fundamental principles include: 1) Qubits (Quantum Bits): Unlike classical bits that are deterministically 0 or 1, qubits exist in a linear superposition |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are complex probability amplitudes such that |α|² + |β|² = 1. 2) Quantum Entanglement: Multiple qubits can become entangled such that the quantum state of each particle cannot be described independently of the others; a system of N entangled qubits can simultaneously represent 2^N states. 3) Quantum Interference: Quantum algorithms choreograph constructive interference to amplify correct computational paths and destructive interference to cancel out incorrect ones. 4) Key Algorithms: Shor's algorithm provides exponential speedup for integer factorization (challenging RSA cryptography), and Grover's algorithm provides quadratic speedup for unstructured database searches.

sources.name: Quantum Computation and Quantum Information
